cues.text: A Vocation Discerned by Another
Born in 1580 (some sources say 1581) at Verdú, in Catalonia, Peter entered the Jesuit novitiate at Tarragona at twenty.

While studying philosophy in Majorca, he came under the spiritual influence of the humble lay brother and doorkeeper St. Alphonsus Rodriguez , who became convinced Peter was called to missionary work in the Americas and never ceased urging him toward it.
Cartagena, the Chief Slave Port
Peter arrived in Cartagena , in modern Colombia, in 1610.
The city, by its position on the Caribbean, had become the principal port through which the transatlantic slave trade delivered captive Africans to the Spanish colonies.
As many as a thousand enslaved people landed there each month, packed into ships under conditions so brutal that a substantial portion did not survive the crossing.
'The Slave of the Negroes Forever'

Trained by the veteran missionary Alonso de Sandoval, who had already spent decades in this same ministry, Peter formally declared himself, by vow, and devoted himself entirely to the enslaved arriving at Cartagena's harbor.

Whenever a slave ship was sighted, he rowed out personally to meet it, bringing food and comfort to people arriving traumatized, sick, and terrified, tending to their physical wounds before attempting any instruction in the faith.
"the slave of the Negroes forever"
Overcoming the Barrier of Language

Recognizing that genuine catechesis required communication in the enslaved people's own languages, Peter assembled a team of interpreters drawn from various African nations and trained them as catechists.
It was an innovative and painstaking approach that allowed him to instruct and baptize hundreds of thousands of individuals over his roughly four decades of ministry.
A Legacy Set Within a Larger Failure
Peter's heroic personal charity must be understood within a deeply troubling wider context.
Though several popes had already condemned the slave trade in principle, the practice continued to flourish throughout his lifetime and for centuries after.

The Society of Jesus itself, in Cartagena and elsewhere in the Americas, held enslaved people during this same era — a history the Jesuit order has in recent years formally acknowledged and sought to address.
Peter Claver could not end slavery; his ministry alleviated individual suffering within a system the Church's own institutions were, in various ways, entangled in.
Legacy
Weakened by years of relentless labor and eventually confined by illness for the final four years of his life, largely neglected by the very community he had served, Peter died at Cartagena in 1654.

Canonized in 1888 alongside his mentor Alphonsus Rodriguez, he was declared patron of missions to Africa by Pope Leo XIII in 1896 and remains honored today as patron of enslaved and formerly enslaved peoples and of interracial justice.
